title: FSSAI seizes 3,280 tonne food items, cancels 52 licences in nationwide inspection drive
author: PTI
content_html:
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has seized 3,280 tonnes of 'banned and non-compliant' food products worth ₹82 crore during its nationwide inspection drive, which began on September 1 to check adulteration during the festive season.

Acting against food safety violations, the FSSAI cancelled 52 licences, suspended 1,133 licences, and sealed 314 establishments.

In a social media post on Saturday (November 7, 2026), the FSSAI said that it has stepped up vigilance in view of festivals.

The regulator said it inspected 56,431 food establishments during its nationwide enforcement drive between September 1 and November 5, and seized non-compliant food products, including paneer, ghee, milk and sweets.

FSSAI led an intensive nationwide inspection drive across States and UTs. Through rigorous checks on over 56,000 food establishments, authorities took decisive action against substandard practices-issuing over 10000 improvement notices and suspending more than 1,100 licences 1(2) https://t.co/Ov7iIZcmdA

— FSSAI (@fssaiindia) November 7, 2026

A total of 3,279.57 tonnes of 'banned and non-compliant' food products worth ₹81.80 crore were seized, it said.

Additionally, the regulator issued 10,047 improvement notices to food business operators.

This calendar year, the FSSAI has stepped up enforcement actions against food business operators and e-commerce companies to ensure safe food for consumers.

title: Deportation of wanted Punjab gangster Afridi secured after 10-month international manhunt
author: PTI
content_html:
Punjab Police, with the support of central agencies, has secured the deportation of wanted gangster Gurwinder alias Afridi from Ethiopia following a 10-month international manhunt.

Punjab DGP Gaurav Yadav on Sunday (November 8, 2026) said the Punjab government had announced a reward of ₹5 lakh for information leading to his arrest.

"In a major breakthrough, Anti-Gangster Task Force (#AGTF) Punjab, in coordination with the Overseas Fugitive Tracking and Extradition Cell (#OFTEC) of Counter Intelligence, Punjab with the support of central agencies, secures the deportation of Gurwinder alias Afridi, a key kingpin of the Doni Bal-Prabh Dassuwal gang, from Ethiopia following a 10-month-long international manhunt under Operation SHAHID," the DGP said in a post on X.

In a major breakthrough, Anti-Gangster Task Force (#AGTF) Punjab, in coordination with the Overseas Fugitive Tracking and Extradition Cell (#OFTEC) of Counter Intelligence, Punjab with the support of Central Agencies, secures the deportation of Gurwinder alias Afridi, a key kingpin of the Doni Bal–Prabh Dassuwal gang, from Ethiopia following a 10-month-long international manhunt under Operation SHAHID. Preliminary investigation reveals that the accused was allegedly directing targeted killings, extortion-related firing incidents and organised criminal activities in Punjab from abroad. The Punjab Government had announced a reward of ₹5 lakh on the information leading to his arrest. The operation involved sustained intelligence gathering, surveillance and tracking across multiple countries in Asia, South-America and Africa, in close coordination with national and international agencies. We thank the Ministry of External Affairs and all other central agencies as part of this international cooperation. @PunjabPoliceInd remains committed to dismantling gangster networks, preventing organised crime and ensuring peace and security across #Punjab.

— DGP Punjab Police (@DGPPunjabPolice) November 8, 2026

He said preliminary investigation reveals that the accused was allegedly directing targeted killings, extortion-related firing incidents and organised criminal activities in Punjab from abroad.

The operation involved sustained intelligence gathering, surveillance and tracking across multiple countries in Asia, South America and Africa, in close coordination with national and international agencies, DGP said.

"We thank the Ministry of External Affairs and all other central agencies as part of this international cooperation," he said.

He added that Punjab Police remains committed to dismantling gangster networks, preventing organised crime and ensuring peace and security across the State.

title: 301 Colony residents put forward 10 recommendations to foster tribal settlement’s development
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
A tribal council meeting (Ooru Koottam) held recently at 301 Colony in Chinnakkanal panchayat near Munnar —one of the regions in the State most prone to wild elephant attacks — put forward ten key recommendations to foster the tribal settlement’s development and long-term sustainability.

The meeting took place on November 3 in the presence of the Adimaly Tribal Development Officer and the site in-charge of the Tribal Rehabilitation and Development Mission (TRDM). During the discussions, residents outlined key priorities spanning housing, basic infrastructure, land utilisation, agriculture, and human-wildlife conflict mitigation. Key proposals include a modern community hall-cum-library, a model preschool, cluster housing, and protective fencing around the settlement to deter wild elephant intrusions.

The council proposed constructing cluster homes on land reserved for public utility, fortified with trenches and fences to prevent animal intrusions. It also requested accommodations for beneficiaries who prefer building on individual plots rather than in clusters. Additionally, the meeting urged the Scheduled Tribes Development department to deliver essential amenities, including electricity, paved roads, drinking water, walkways, and retaining walls, as well as to renovate dilapidated houses through relevant department schemes.

The council also called on authorities to cancel the title deeds (pattayams) of allottees who have not yet occupied their plots, and to reallocate the land to eligible landless families. Beneficiaries who have leased out their plots were instructed to terminate the agreements, reclaim their land, and take up farming. If they fail to comply, the District Collector will be petitioned to initiate eviction proceedings and repossess the plots.

Agri cooperative society

Furthermore, the council recommended establishing an agricultural cooperative society once all beneficiaries take possession of their plots to help market local produce. The Tribal Development Officer stated that registration procedures would begin by electing a 15-member committee of beneficiaries. The council also called for streamlining administrative processes to transfer plot ownership to the legal heirs of deceased titleholders and to issue replacement deeds for lost documents.

The Tribal Development Officer reiterated that all individuals who leased out allotted plots must reclaim the land, cultivate it, and establish permanent residence, warning that non-compliance would result in deed cancellations and reallotments. Colony residents agreed to reclaim leased holdings and settle permanently.

According to officials, 211 of the 301 families have already settled in the colony. The remaining 90 families have been unable to construct homes due to various hardships, including deaths in the family.

In 2002–03, the A.K. Antony government allotted one acre of land each to 301 tribal families. However, the decision has long faced criticism because the area lies within a natural elephant corridor, making wild elephant encounters a recurring threat for the settlement. Recently, the Forest Minister admitted that permitting human settlement in 301 Colony across natural elephant corridors in Chinnakkanal was a grave mistake made by the government.

title: Keralam measles outbreaks call for a relook at disease epidemiology
author: C Maya
content_html:
As Keralam grapples with measles outbreaks across districts, particularly Kozhikode, Malappuram and Palakkad, public health experts are calling for a detailed reassessment of the disease’s epidemiology, which appears to have changed significantly over the years.

Once predominantly a childhood disease affecting children aged one to five, measles is now being reported across age groups, including among fully vaccinated individuals and infants below nine months, who are not yet eligible for routine measles vaccination.

The last major surge in cases was in 2022-23. As of November 6, the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme had reported 824 confirmed and 1,681 probable measles cases in the State. Five measles-related deaths have been reported, though only one has been confirmed so far.

In UIP

Measles vaccination was introduced into the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) in 1985, with a single dose at nine months. A second dose, at 18 months, was introduced in 2010 to address immunity gaps following the first dose and support measles elimination.

The nine-month threshold was intended to ensure that maternal antibodies transferred through the placenta did not interfere with the vaccine-induced immune response. However, the changing age profile of recent outbreaks raises questions about whether this protection strategy remains adequate.

“In recent epidemics, we have seen a good number of infants developing measles before nine months, potentially because mothers of the present generation have lower levels of measles antibodies. We also have a chunk of cases among older adults,” says K.K. Purushothaman, former Professor of Paediatrics at Government Medical College, Thrissur.

He believes the State should consider an additional dose of a measles-containing vaccine under the UIP, either during adolescence or for women before marriage. The State Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation should examine the proposal and commission serological studies among adolescents and young women to assess their protective antibody levels, he says.

The concern is supported by findings elsewhere. Following major measles outbreaks in Mumbai in 2023, when more than 31% of reported cases were among infants below nine months, a seroprevalence study found that only 66.8% of mothers had adequate measles antibodies to protect their infants.

Measles antibodies

A World Health Organisation (WHO) informal technical consultation report, published in Vaccine in May 2025, acknowledged that women acquiring immunity through vaccination rather than natural infection might transfer lower levels of measles antibodies to their babies. However, experts concluded that evidence was insufficient to change the existing recommendation for the first routine dose at 9-15 months.

Meanwhile, research closer home suggests that vaccination history alone may not fully explain the emerging picture. A study by the Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (RGCB), involving 684 children aged four to 18 from Keralam and Tamil Nadu, who had received at least two doses of a measles-containing vaccine, assessed their measles antibody levels. Antibodies were also measured in 544 mothers.

Published in JAMA Network Open in August 2025, the study found that 8.5% of the children lacked antibody levels classified as protective. Another 89 children (13%) tested positive for measles-specific IgM, which can indicate recent infection, while 90 (13.2%) had borderline results. The researchers interpreted these findings as suggestive of recent measles exposure and possible breakthrough infections.

Notably, 435 children (63.6%) had received a third vaccine dose, while seven had received a fourth, yet antibody responses varied. The findings raise questions about the durability and adequacy of vaccine-induced immunity, although antibody levels alone do not establish whether an individual will develop clinical measles.

Keralam generally reports around 95% coverage for the first dose of the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine. Coverage of the second dose, administered at 18 months, has consistently been lower, at around 85-88%, with some districts reporting still poorer coverage.

Incomplete immunisation

Incomplete immunisation remains a major driver of outbreaks. The Health department has often attributed outbreaks to districts such as Malappuram and Kozhikode, where vaccination gaps are substantial. However, experts point out that pockets of under-immunisation exist across the State and cases are being reported in every district, among unvaccinated, partially vaccinated and fully vaccinated children.

The RGCB findings also challenge the assumption that high vaccination coverage alone guarantees adequate population immunity. The WHO’s elimination strategy depends on high two-dose coverage, effective surveillance and rapid outbreak response. Further research is needed to understand the reasons for variable antibody responses among vaccinated children.

Keralam now needs larger epidemiological investigations to establish how many laboratory-confirmed cases occurred among children with two verified vaccine doses, those with partial or no immunisation and the age-break-up of those affected. Such evidence would help determine whether current outbreaks are driven predominantly by incomplete coverage or whether additional immunity gaps also need to be addressed.
